chunks: From him, from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, from Ali (peace be upon him), who said:

I was with Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), and Abu Basir asked him: 'The night in which what is hoped for is hoped for?' He said: 'On the twenty-first or the twenty-third.' Abu Basir said: 'If I cannot manage both?' He said: 'How easy are two nights for what you are seeking.' I said: 'Perhaps we see the new moon here, and someone comes to inform us of the opposite in another land?' He said: 'How easy are four nights to seek in them.' I said: 'May I be your ransom, the night of the twenty-third is the night of al-Juhani?' He said: 'Indeed, that is said.' I said: 'Sulayman ibn Khalid narrated regarding the nineteenth, that the delegation of the pilgrims is written?' He said: 'O Abu Muhammad, the delegation of the pilgrims is written on the Night of Decree, along with destinies, calamities, provisions, and whatever occurs like it in the coming year. So seek them in the twenty-first and twenty-third, and pray one hundred rak'ahs in each of them, and keep them awake if you can.' I said: 'And if I cannot?' He said: 'It is not a problem for you to close your eyes in the beginning of the night with some sleep. Indeed, the gates of heaven are opened in Ramadan, the devils are chained, and the deeds of the believers are accepted. What a good month is Ramadan; it was called al-Marzooq (the Provisioned) during the time of the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family).'

key_terms.وَفْدُ الْحَاجِّ: Delegation of the pilgrims (referring to the writing of deeds)

ai.seo_question: Which nights in Ramadan are most likely to be Laylat al-Qadr according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) identifies the 21st, 23rd, and 19th nights as the primary candidates for Laylat al-Qadr, noting that divine decrees for the coming year—including sustenance and events—are inscribed on these nights. The narration emphasizes the immense virtue of these nights by recommending 100 rak'ahs of prayer, while offering leniency for those unable to maintain full wakefulness, reflecting the Shia scholarly tradition of balancing rigorous devotion with practical accessibility. It further highlights Ramadan's historical title 'Al-Marzooq' (the Sustained One), underscoring its role as the month where Allah’s provisions are decreed and accepted.
